## About

Service Architect is a visual designer and code generator for distributed systems. You draw a graph of services, typed pipelines, and connections; the designer generates the Rust workspace, transport adapters, configuration, observability wiring, and runtime graph.

This repository is the Rust runtime used by that generated code. The Go implementation is the semantic reference, while this port uses Rust ownership, `Arc`, Tokio tasks, and async transports without changing observable stream, cancellation, lifecycle, configuration, or connector behavior.

> **The graph is the architecture. It runs the system and remains accurate by definition.**

ServiceLib is normally consumed through generated projects rather than assembled by hand.

→ **[Open Service Architect](https://www.gorundebug.com)**

---

## What The Runtime Provides

- Strongly typed stream graphs generated from the Service Architect model
- Tokio-based asynchronous execution and lifecycle management
- Function-call, task-pool, priority-pool, and parallel call semantics
- HTTP, gRPC, Kafka, and local in-process connectors
- Deadlines, cancellation propagation, delay pools, and graceful shutdown
- In-memory join state with rotating retention maps
- OpenTelemetry traces and logs, Prometheus-compatible metrics, and status endpoints
- Layered YAML configuration with environment overrides and transactional hot reload

Messages keep `MessageContext` and `Payload<T>` separate. `Payload<T>` uses `Arc<T>` so asynchronous calls and split branches can share immutable values without eager deep copies.

---

## Execution Model

Generated services build their graph once during startup. Runtime requests then move through pre-wired consumers using the call semantics selected for each link:

| Semantics | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `FunctionCall` | Invoke the next consumer directly; optionally dispatch asynchronously |
| `TaskPool` | Schedule work on a named bounded worker pool |
| `PriorityTaskPool` | Schedule work on a named pool using request priority |
| `Parallel` | Dispatch independently through the Tokio runtime |

Graph construction, consumer resolution, dispatch order, middleware chains, and metric instruments are prepared before request processing. The hot path executes the graph; it does not rebuild it.

---

## Operators

| Operator | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Input` | Receive data from an external system |
| `Sink` | Send data to an external system |
| `Map` / `Filter` | Transform or conditionally pass values |
| `FlatMap` / `FlatMapIterable` | Expand a value into multiple outputs |
| `Process` / `Error` | Produce normal and error output streams |
| `KeyBy` | Partition values by key |
| `Join` / `MultiJoin` | Combine keyed streams |
| `Merge` / `Split` | Merge or fan out stream branches |
| `Case` / `When` | Route values conditionally |
| `Delay` | Deliver later or immediately on cancellation |
| `CycleLink` | Feed values back into the graph |

---

## Connectors

**Sources** — HTTP · gRPC (unary and streaming) · Kafka · local in-process

**Sinks** — HTTP · gRPC (unary and streaming) · Kafka · local in-process

HTTP and gRPC propagate stream identity, trace context, baggage, and remaining deadlines where the transport supports them. Process-local scheduling metadata, such as priority, stays local.

---

## Configuration And Hot Reload

Configuration is assembled in this order:

```text
generated defaults → base YAML → overrides YAML → environment variables → validation
```

When an overrides file is configured, ServiceLib watches its directory and supports both direct writes and atomic replacements such as Kubernetes ConfigMap updates. A candidate snapshot is validated completely before publication. Failed reloads are logged and counted while the last valid configuration remains active.

Runtime snapshots are published through `ArcSwap`; task pools and priority pools reload their settings without rebuilding the service graph.

---

## Observability

The default runtime exposes its Prometheus registry through the generated service metrics endpoint. OTLP metrics, traces, and structured logs can share one OpenTelemetry installation:

```rust
use servicelib::runtime::{
    config::CallSemantics,
    environment::RuntimeEnvironment,
    telemetry::opentelemetry::{Config, OpenTelemetry},
};

let telemetry = OpenTelemetry::install(Config::from_environment("orders"))?;
let environment = RuntimeEnvironment::with_telemetry(
    CallSemantics::FunctionCall,
    telemetry.clone(),
    telemetry.clone(),
    telemetry,
);
```

Request tracing is enabled by a non-empty `X-Trace`/`x-trace` marker or an already sampled W3C remote parent. Without either signal, ServiceLib avoids creating recording request, operator, pool, source, or sink spans.

Tests can use `runtime::testmetrics`, `runtime::testlog`, and `runtime::testtracing`, which implement the same lifecycle contracts as the production engines.

## Framework API Generation

[`servicelib/api/serviceapi.yaml`](https://github.com/gorundebug/servicelib/blob/main/api/serviceapi.yaml) in the Go repository is the canonical cross-language framework schema. In the development workspace:

```sh
make api
make api-check
```

The generated Rust API is committed so standalone checkouts do not need the Go repository.

---

## Testing

Run the reproducible Docker test suite:

```sh
./scripts/test.sh
```

Or, with a matching local Rust toolchain:

```sh
cargo test --all-targets
```
